name: Emeka Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a crew chief on new line construction for the power company. These days that means building the big lines that connect the wind farms and the solar parks to the grid, so I spend a lot of my week on sites out in the country, living out of a hotel from Monday to Thursday. A normal day, we're setting steel poles with a crane, or pulling new conductor through a line of towers with a tension machine, which is slow, careful work. I'm in charge of twelve people, and my main job is making sure every one of them goes home at night the same shape they arrived.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy building something that will be there for fifty years. I can drive my grandchildren past a line one day and say, your grandfather built that. What wears me out is the hotels and the food, and being away from my wife Grace, who runs a catering business and feeds half the church on Sundays. I'm a deacon at our church, so my weekends are not exactly quiet either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always think the next new thing will change the world, and usually it just changes the paperwork. At church I'd say hard work and good people still matter most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's good. I'd keep building lines till sixty-two, then let Grace finally teach me to cook, which she's been threatening for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep putting money aside, keep the rental house we own let out, help Grace with the business when she needs a driver. I'd still use the AI now and then, it's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger son Obi showed me how to use the chatbot on my phone. I use it to check the specifications on a job, and to help write the church newsletter, which is easier than it was. I don't trust it with anything important, mind you, I check everything twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your son Chidi make of AI? You mentioned he's in the trade too.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He uses it more than me. He says it's good for paperwork and useless for climbing. He's thirty-two, a lineworker with another company, so he'd be glad, I think, that his job stayed steady.

S0.say: He'd say he's not surprised, because new things usually just change the paperwork. At church he'd say hard work and good people still matter most.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changes for him, which is good: he'd build lines until sixty-two and then finally let his wife teach him to cook.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, keeps the family rental house let out and helps his wife's catering business when she needs a driver. Continues using AI now and then for specifications and the church newsletter.
S0.quote: I'd keep building lines till sixty-two, then let Grace finally teach me to cook, which she's been threatening for thirty years.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is a steady, warm crew chief and church deacon whose first concern is that every crew member goes home safe. He uses AI now and then but checks everything twice. His pride in building lines that will last fifty years runs through his answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and we'll adjust, like we did with the computers and the tension machines. At work I'd say learn what you need to learn, but don't forget the basics. At church I'd say families and communities need to look after each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be okay. We're building more lines than ever with all the wind and solar, so there's work for years. If anything, I'd worry the robots arrive just as the boom is ending, and the young ones get the worst of both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the training when it's been tried by the other crews and the problems are sorted out. I'd keep saving the same, keep working to sixty-two, and encourage my crew to learn new skills alongside the old ones. I'd use the AI a bit more for planning and paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little concern for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be one of the first to learn the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, second wave. Let the eager ones find the problems first, then I'll learn it properly. I've seen too many new machines turn up on site and break down in the first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade properly, and learn the new tools too. Save your money, don't spend it all on new trucks and holidays. And get an apprenticeship, because that's how you learn the work properly, not from a video.

S1.say: He'd say change is part of life and they'll adjust, as they did with computers and tension machines. At church he'd say families and communities need to look after each other.
S1.think: He thinks he'd be okay because the wind and solar boom means years of work. His worry is robots arriving just as the boom ends, hurting the young ones twice.
S1.do: Takes training once other crews have tried the new systems and sorted the problems. Keeps saving and working to sixty-two, uses AI more for planning and paperwork, and encourages his crew to learn new skills alongside old ones.
S1.feel: Calm, with a little concern for the young ones.
S1.quote: If anything, I'd worry the robots arrive just as the boom is ending, and the young ones get the worst of both.
S1.fieldNote: He's a second-wave adopter who waits for others to find the problems. He sees the clean energy building boom as a buffer for himself, but worries about younger workers if it ends just as robots arrive. His advice to the young is thrift and apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and the people pushing it don't care about the people it hurts. At church I'd say we need to pray and pull together and look after our families. At work I'd say stay calm and do your job until they tell you otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me. I'd be sixty, I could stop, but Chidi would be thirty-four with a mortgage and two little ones. I'd have spent my life building lines for machines that don't need me, and my son would be standing next to me with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Grace in the first month and go over our savings, the rental house and the business. We'd put more aside and stop any big spending. I'd tell Chidi that if he loses his job, we can help with the mortgage for a while, and I'd see what the company offers before deciding whether to go early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but heavy in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Chidi in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be in trouble, like a lot of young men. I'd want him to go back to the basics: family, church, and finding something useful to do with his hands. I'd tell him to save every penny and not take on any new debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace runs a catering business. How does that fare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably hit too. A lot of her work is lunches for offices, and if the offices empty, so does her order book. But people still have weddings and funerals, and they still want real food made by a person, so she'd keep some of it.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast and the people pushing it don't care who gets hurt. At church he'd urge prayer and pulling together, and at work he'd tell people to stay calm and do their jobs.
S2.think: He'd be sixty and able to stop, but his son would be thirty-four with a mortgage and two small children. He'd feel he had spent his life building lines for machines that don't need people.
S2.do: Goes over savings, the rental house and the catering business with his wife in the first month, saving more and cutting big spending. Offers to help his son with the mortgage for a while and waits to see what the company offers before deciding whether to retire early.
S2.feel: Anxious, not panicking, but heavy in his chest.
S2.quote: I'd have spent my life building lines for machines that don't need me, and my son would be standing next to me with nothing to do.
S2.fieldNote: His own money is safe, but he worries most about his son, a lineworker with young children. His response combines family support with faith and thrift. The image of father and son standing idle by the lines they built was the most painful thing he said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's prepare. At work I'd say learn the new systems and save your money. At church I'd say families should talk now, not wait for the trouble to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired just before it lands. It's better than the fast one, but I'd still worry about Chidi and Obi. Five years is long enough to prepare, but not so long that anyone can pretend it's not coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new systems once the first crews have them working, so I can teach my crew. I'd keep saving and help Chidi think about what he might move into, maybe robot maintenance, maybe something else. I'd retire at sixty-two as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but steady. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change what you'd tell Chidi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell him to start saving harder now, and to get some training on the robots as soon as the company offers it. I'd tell him to keep his family close and not take on new debt. He's a good lad, he'd listen, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your own plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd stick to my date. I might put a little more aside for the grandchildren's schooling, in case their parents have a hard time.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to prepare, so prepare: learn the new systems and save. At church he'd urge families to talk now rather than wait for trouble.
S3.think: He thinks he'd be retired just before it lands, which is better than the fast picture, but he'd still worry about his sons. Five years is long enough to prepare and too short to pretend it isn't coming.
S3.do: Learns the new systems once the first crews have them working so he can teach his crew. Keeps saving, helps his son consider moving into robot maintenance, sets a little extra aside for his grandchildren's schooling and retires at sixty-two as planned.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy but steady, with time to act.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to prepare, but not so long that anyone can pretend it's not coming.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years ease his own worry and turn his attention to coaching his son. His steady approach to technology becomes a way to teach his crew. Saving for grandchildren's schooling shows how he thinks across generations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare, if they're sensible. At church I'd say save, learn and look after each other. At work I'd say start learning now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing really. I'd be long retired. By 2036 I'll be the man in the church car park telling the young ones how we pulled cable by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going till sixty-two, keep using the AI for the odd thing, and help my sons plan. I'd encourage Chidi to get training on the new systems early, and I'd keep our savings safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little sorry for the trade, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years give your sons enough time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so, if they use it. Chidi would have time to move into something new, maybe supervising the robots. Obi works in insurance, and I don't know what happens to that. I'd tell them both to keep learning and not to rely on anyone else to look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandchildren to understand about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it was hard, honest work, and it kept the lights on in their homes. Every time they switch on a light, somebody climbed something for it. I'd want them to remember that.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare if people are sensible. At church he'd say save, learn and look after each other, and at work start learning now.
S4.think: He thinks nothing really changes for him since he'd be long retired. He'd be the man in the church car park telling stories about pulling cable by hand.
S4.do: Works until sixty-two and keeps using AI for the odd task. Helps his sons plan, encourages his elder son to train early on the new systems, and keeps the family savings safe.
S4.feel: Calm, a little sorry for the trade.
S4.quote: Every time they switch on a light, somebody climbed something for it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he relaxes, confident his sons have time if they use it. He admits he doesn't know what happens to his younger son's insurance job. His pride in honest work and his hope that grandchildren remember who kept the lights on are central to him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of my sons and their families. What would help is companies being honest early about what's coming, keeping apprenticeships going, and helping people move into new work. And families and churches being ready to help each other, because I don't trust the government to be quick enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who will build the lines for all these robots and data centres. They'll need a lot of power, and somebody has to build the lines to carry it. For a few years at least, that might be the busiest work in the country.

headlineQuote: By 2036 I'll be the man in the church car park telling the young ones how we pulled cable by hand.
portrait: Emeka Okafor is a 58-year-old crew chief building new transmission lines to connect wind and solar farms, spending his weeks in hotels and his weekends as a church deacon. He's steady and thrifty, uses AI now and then but checks everything twice, and believes in apprenticeships, family and hard work. With savings, a rental house and his wife's catering business, he's calm in the plateau and steady change pictures. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, mostly for his son, a lineworker with young children, while five and ten years give him time to coach his sons and retire as planned.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because of what it would mean for his sons and their families.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being honest early, keeping apprenticeships going and helping people move into new work, with families and churches ready to help each other.
